item.title: She Killed Her 4-Year-Old Girl. Can She Ever Be Considered Sane?
item.description:
Sixteen years ago, Marci Webber killed her 4-year-old daughter, Maggie, in the midst of a psychotic episode, then cut her own wrists. When Ms. Webber’s eldest daughter, then 18, found them in the bathroom, Ms. Webber told her, “Shhh, don’t wake the baby.”

She has been institutionalized in Illinois ever since, but for over a decade she has argued that she no longer needs inpatient care. In November, a judge will decide whether she can go free.

The particulars of Ms. Webber’s case are different from those of Lindsay Clancy, whose recent trial on charges of killing her three young children resulted in a hung jury. Ms. Clancy is scheduled to have a hearing to determine next steps in her case next month. But Ms. Webber’s case offers a look at what long-term institutionalization and involuntary treatment can mean for someone found not guilty by reason of insanity.

Ms. Clancy’s trial lasted three weeks, during which the jury saw autopsy photos and children’s pajamas, and even took a trip to the crime scene. Defense lawyers argued that she was insane, and persuaded all but one juror that she should be found not guilty. Now the prosecutor must decide whether to put her on trial again.

Ms. Webber’s trial, on the other hand, took one day and had one witness, a forensic psychologist. She chose not to have a jury. A judge in DuPage County, the suburban county outside Chicago where the killing occurred, found her not guilty by reason of insanity.

The result has been years of debate and hearings over the role of medications and whether she is stable enough to live outside of a mental health facility. As Ms. Webber has tried to win her freedom, the court has heard conflicting testimony on Ms. Webber’s diagnosis, treatment, behavior and what she says are attempts to force her to take psychiatric drugs.

Prosecutors say Ms. Webber fails to fully grasp the harm she caused, in part because she blames medications, not mental illness, for Maggie’s death.

Involuntary commitment for those found not guilty by reason of insanity is supposed to be for treatment, not punishment. In Illinois, patients may be committed for no longer than what their prison sentence would have been if found guilty — in Ms. Webber’s case, 100 years. There is no minimum.

In many states, such patients receive periodic assessments to determine if inpatient treatment is still needed. In Illinois, a patient may petition the court for release.

In phone interviews from the state hospital where she is being held in Illinois., Ms. Webber spoke of how acutely she missed Maggie. “She was everything to me,” she said.

Years of imprisonment or institutionalization, she argued, will not prevent more children from dying at the hands of their parents. “These mothers are trying to protect their child from something in their heads.”

Ms. Webber, an Army veteran, began taking an antidepressant in the mid-1990s when she was embroiled in a custody dispute with the father of her eldest daughter. Over the years, she was prescribed a host of other antidepressants and antipsychotics, along with a beta blocker sometimes used to treat acute anxiety.

Millions of Americans use medication to treat mental health disorders, and they are considered both safe and effective. A regimen involving several drugs is not necessarily a red flag — experts said it can be desirable in complex illnesses.

But Ms. Webber’s case raises questions that also arose in the Clancy trial, about whether a shifting regimen of psychiatric drugs can contribute to violence. Psychiatric drugs can have adverse effects, particularly when treatment is initiated, doses are changed, or medications are discontinued. If unaddressed, experts say, these side effects may increase the risk of suicide or violence.

Ms. Webber said she had experienced akathisia, an involuntary and sometimes torturous restlessness.

“What they did for years was add meds, switch meds and just continue on,” Ms. Webber said. ‘Nobody thought to say, ‘You know what? I think she’s allergic to this stuff.’”

Dr. Gerard Sanacora, director of the Yale Depression Research Program, said it can be difficult to tease out whether conditions like psychosis are the result of disorders or the drugs being used to treat them.

“These medications are much more likely to help somebody than hurt somebody, but that doesn’t mean that an individual can’t be harmed,” he said.

Ms. Webber was raising three daughters and attending law school in upstate New York when she became obsessively religious, attending Mass daily and traveling 100 miles to a prayer group on weekends, children in tow. When she spotted a praying mantis at a gas station she “rescued” it, believing it was a sign.

Her older daughters had been named after a sitcom character and a president. She named Maggie after Mary Magdalene.

In the Clancy trial, prosecutors sought to portray the defendant as manipulative and controlling, saying she had meticulously planned her children’s death as she had planned their meals and activities.

Ms. Webber said such evidence proved nothing.

“Planning has nothing to do with whether a person is psychotic and insane,” she said. “You will have things that you’re doing that seem totally normal, but on the inside — unless people ask questions — you’re not normal.”

In 2010, Ms. Webber was increasingly worried for Maggie’s safety, believing that she was the target of sexual predators, and moved the girl to her grandmother’s townhouse in Illinois.

Ms. Webber was convinced that Satanists had rented the surrounding properties, and that she was being followed. She kept a knife under her mattress for protection. She felt evil as a physical sensation on her skin.

On a trip to the grocery store, she remembers asking others, “Is there a pill we can take to end our lives if they capture us?”

“You think you can handle it,” she said, “You think, ‘Oh, it’s going to go away or something.’ Until it’s too late.”

Relatives noticed that something was wrong, but Ms. Webber denied it. She now wishes they had asked more questions. She is no longer in touch with her family and asked that they not be contacted, saying that they had been through enough.

In a recent interview on “60 Minutes,” Patrick Clancy, Ms. Clancy’s former husband, offered a glimpse into what friends and relatives face when trying to respond to a deteriorating mental state. “Mental illness has this ability to be tragically deceptive,” he said.

Ms. Webber was having nightmares and not sleeping. Her paranoia coalesced into “a firm, fixed, false belief,” and she heard a voice telling her that Maggie needed to be saved, she said. She wishes she had been involuntarily hospitalized.

Instead, on Nov. 3, 2010, Ms. Webber’s teenage daughter entered the bathroom to find her sister’s body and the words “divine mercy” written in blood on the wall. Ms. Webber had turned on an audio recorder to capture angels arriving to take her and Maggie to heaven.

In 2014, after the judge’s not guilty verdict and several years of inpatient treatment, Ms. Webber refused psychiatric drugs. Her psychosis did not return, a judge found. Still, in 2017, he denied her release, saying both Ms. Webber and the state needed to do more to prepare. She attempted suicide.

In 2019, that judge released Ms. Webber with a treatment plan, after expressing concern that the state was not treating her fairly.

She returned to her apartment, but prosecutors appealed the judge’s decision and won. After less than two weeks, she returned to the mental institution.

Ms. Webber says that her institutionalization has gone on too long and is harming her physical and mental health.

In one conversation with Ms. Webber, prolonged screaming could be heard in the background. It was a fellow patient who, Ms. Webber said, was in a wheelchair and calling for help.

“God, I can’t stand living like this. Do you hear this?” she asked. “It is the most untherapeutic place you could ever be in.”

Prosecutors have argued that Ms. Webber remains dangerous, citing the suicide attempt, “aggressive, unruly and hostile behavior” and rule infractions. They say that her symptoms improve when she takes medication and worsen when she stops.

Under Illinois law, the burden is now on Ms. Webber to convince a judge that she is not likely to harm herself or others, or would not benefit from continued inpatient care. Her next hearing is in November.

item.title: An Iowa Republican’s Unusual Connection to the Kochs (and Kansas)
item.description:
If there is one thing that Zach Lahn, the Republican nominee for governor of Iowa, definitely does not want to talk about, it’s his connection to the Koch family.

To hear Mr. Lahn tell it, he is a self-made businessman, a father of seven and a farmer running against powerful corporate interests. He has campaigned on his financial independence, pointing to the $2.5 million he lent himself during the primary.

He rode that cash and a right-leaning brand of prairie populism to the nomination, defeating President Trump’s preferred pick in the primary. Now he is facing Rob Sand, the Democratic state auditor, in a race that Democrats view as one of their best shots to flip a governorship.

But there is a more complicated tale of Mr. Lahn’s rise that is interwoven with the Kochs, one of America’s richest and most influential political dynasties.

The story includes years of work for Koch-funded endeavors, a divorce and a new marriage to a former Koch who had just received a sizable divorce settlement of her own. It involves an expanding investment portfolio — including a million-dollar stake in a manufacturer of high-tech penis rings — accusations of carpetbagging and a private plane that has shuttled back and forth to Kansas with two words emblazoned under the wings: “Iowa First.”

“My wife used to be married into the family,” Mr. Lahn, 40, said at a recent town-hall event in Humboldt, Iowa, when asked by a voter about his connection to the Kochs. “But if anyone understands how those situations go, they’re not exactly wanting to support me. I think that’s quite clear.”

In fact, some of the Kochs did not even know his campaign was coming.

At the town hall, Mr. Lahn downplayed his ties to the Kochs. “I have worked for one group that was funded by them one year — for one year — 10 years ago,” he said.

His connections are deeper.

In 2014, Mr. Lahn was hired to lead the Montana chapter of Americans for Prosperity, the conservative advocacy group in the Kochs’ political network. He held the post for about a year and then served as a fund-raiser for the organization into 2016.

At a Koch-funded education conference, he met a woman named Annie Koch, the wife of Chase Koch, son of the billionaire industrialist Charles Koch, one of the nation’s richest men and leading political financiers.

Soon, Mr. Lahn moved to Kansas, where he co-founded a private school with Annie Koch, called Wonder, that was bankrolled by her and her husband.

In 2017, Mr. Lahn started working for the school, which opened in 2018.

Two years later, the Kochs were divorced, and so were Mr. Lahn and his wife. Mr. Lahn and the future Annie Lahn applied for a marriage license 11 days after his divorce was finalized, in June 2020, court records show.

Mr. Lahn’s financial arrangement with the school was unusual.

From 2017 to 2024, he worked 50 hours per week for Wonder, according to Internal Revenue Service records. The records say he was never paid.

“The school was a passion project, 100 percent,” Mr. Lahn said in an interview with The New York Times, adding that the “school never paid me anything.”

He was, however, being paid at the time. Mr. Lahn was directly billing Annie and Chase Koch through a limited liability company, according to an email and invoices later obtained by The Times. Mr. Lahn sent the Kochs monthly bills for “consulting services.”

In 2019, his monthly billings were $20,883, which would add up to an annual salary approaching $250,000. One internal email refers to his compensation as “salary.”

In an email following the interview, Mr. Lahn’s campaign manager, Paul Cordes, stood by Mr. Lahn’s claim that he was never paid by Wonder. Mr. Cordes said the bills were “related to consulting work that also predates the school.”

Mr. Lahn and Annie have also lent money to the school in recent years; tax records last year showed a balance due of about $4.5 million.

Court filings in Mr. Lahn’s divorce offered little hint of the wealth he would later tap into in his run for governor. In the interview, he said the documents did not require him to list all his assets because he went through a “collaborative divorce.”

Many assets, however, were listed, including $6,401 in a retirement account. He reported about $50,000 in joint savings and checking accounts and another $51,000 in a business account. His $210,000 Iowa farmhouse had a $163,750 mortgage balance.

He listed an annual income of $240,000 on one document and an annual income of $380,000 on a child-support worksheet.

The attorney for Mr. Lahn’s ex-wife declined to comment on his finances.

The Kochs’ divorce records are sealed, but a person with knowledge of the settlement, who was granted anonymity to discuss a private agreement, said that Annie received a sum in the eight-figure range.

In the years since marrying Annie, Mr. Lahn’s investment activity surged, mostly through limited liability companies, public records show.

In 2021, he bought a “ski-in, ski-out” lot at the base of a mountain in Whitefish, Mont., valued at $1.5 million, and he bought and sold a home in the same resort valued at $4.5 million. He and Annie bought and sold a three-bedroom home near their farm. He also bought a 1930s-era movie theater in Belle Plaine, Iowa, for $250,000 in 2023 and roughly 435 acres in surrounding Benton County.

In 2021, one of Mr. Lahn’s limited liability companies bought a $1 million stake in FirmTech Inc., a men’s sexual health company that makes penis rings promising longer erections and more intense orgasms. At one point, the company sought to trademark hats that read, “Make America Firm Again.”

Campaign officials say he resigned his position with the company in 2023.

In the interview with The Times, Mr. Lahn noted that before his second marriage, he purchased a Montana apparel company for $3 million, which he said was “100 percent my own money.”

“There’s been plenty of money that I have made prior to the divorce,” he said, citing work for start-up companies and the purchase of rental property in Montana. His campaign declined to provide any details or documentation.

Mr. Lahn bristled at the suggestion that his wife’s divorce settlement had fueled his business career or contributed to the $2.5 million he lent his campaign.

“Silly question,” he called it.

On a windswept day last November, Mr. Lahn began his campaign at the Belle Plaine farmhouse that was built by his great-great-grandfather in 1900. He was surrounded by the seven children he now shares with his wife, Annie.

(The Lahns each had three children from their previous marriages and have since had one child together.)

The event came as a surprise to Chase Koch.

Mr. Koch learned of Mr. Lahn’s campaign — and the supporting role of his children — only when he saw them in media clips, according to two people close to him, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss a sensitive matter.

Mr. Lahn declined to say whether he had alerted Mr. Koch about his children’s role in the campaign kickoff.

“We’ve had good communication on this, but I’m not talking about the kids or the family,” he said, adding, “Our family dealings are our family dealings.”

A representative for Mr. Koch declined to comment, citing the children’s privacy.

Mr. Lahn’s residency has emerged as one of the most fraught issues of the race, with Mr. Sand repeatedly accusing him of being a “Kansas carpetbagger.”

Mr. Lahn has said that he lives full-time in Iowa but that his children split their time between the two states.

Flight records first reported by The Des Moines Register showed Mr. Lahn’s private plane frequently shuttling between the states.

“The airplane goes back and forth to pick up the kids as they split time,” Mr. Lahn, a pilot, said in the interview, adding that he was not always flying the plane with “Iowa First” under the wings.

The Lahns also own a 26-acre Frank Lloyd Wright-inspired estate appraised at $1.8 million — complete with an indoor pool and a private lake — just north of Wichita, Kan.

Mr. Sand has aired a pointed TV ad that calls him an “Iowa public school dad.” Mr. Lahn has repeatedly berated Mr. Sand for what he framed as attacks on his children, who attend school in Kansas.

“I am not going to be intimidated on this,” Mr. Lahn said in a heated exchange during a recent debate, vowing to “defend my children from people who’d like to exploit them like you.”

Mr. Sand responded: “This is not about why you’re in Kansas. This is about the fact that you’re not in Iowa.”

Mr. Lahn voted in Iowa years ago but voted in Kansas in 2018, 2020 and 2022. He re-registered in Iowa in October 2024 — just in time to qualify to run for office in 2026.

Mr. Lahn cast an Iowa ballot in the 2024 general election. But voting records that have not previously been reported show he requested that his ballot be mailed to him — in Kansas.

“All my official mail has gone to my assistant for years,” he explained.

Mr. Lahn has tried to turn the tables on the question of familial wealth.

He has repeatedly invoked Mr. Sand’s wife and her family, who for years have been his major political benefactors.

Mr. Sand is married to Christine Lauridsen, who leads her family’s conglomerate, Lauridsen Group, Inc. She and her family have contributed about $5.8 million to Mr. Sand’s campaign for governor.

“He is a billionaire,” Mr. Lahn claimed in a recent ad. “He doesn’t get what regular folks go through.”

Mr. Sand’s campaign declined to respond to the criticism.

Mr. Lahn’s line of attack has puzzled some political observers who are aware of Mr. Lahn’s connection to the Koch family.

“It seems like the objective is more to muddy the waters,” said Eric Woolson, a Republican consultant in Iowa. “I don’t know that it’s going to resonate with most Iowa voters.”

At the Humboldt town hall, Mr. Lahn dismissed talk of his Koch connections as “conspiratorial” and stressed his opposition to the role played by the family’s multinational conglomerate in the agricultural industry.

“They’re not supporting me in any way, shape or form,” he said. “Not a dollar of inside help, a dollar of outside help. Nothing.”

The Koch super PAC, Americans for Prosperity Action Inc., has spent more than $13.3 million on Iowa’s Senate race this year.

The group has spent nothing for Mr. Lahn.

Kitty Bennett contributed research.

item.title: Democrats Have Edge Across Four Key House Races in Pennsylvania, Polls Find
item.description:
Democrats trying to unseat Republicans in four battleground Pennsylvania House districts are ahead in two of them, hold a narrow edge in a third and are tied in a fourth, according to new polling from The New York Times, The Philadelphia Inquirer and Siena University.

The four seats in Pennsylvania are seen as critical examples of some of the fights playing out nationwide. The districts include working-class communities in the state’s northeastern corner, growing towns with large Hispanic populations, a swing Philadelphia suburb and some more conservative parts of the center of the state.

In the 2024 election, Pennsylvania was one of the country’s biggest battlegrounds, and Republicans romped nearly everywhere. President Trump carried the state en route to being re-elected, and it was the only state in the country where Republicans flipped two House seats.

But the new polls show that Democrats are now leading in their bid to flip back both of those districts.

Taken together, the findings in the races for the four seats amount to another warning sign for a Republican Party that is increasingly at risk of losing its narrow House majority.

In Pennsylvania’s Eighth District, Representative Rob Bresnahan, a Republican, trails his Democratic challenger, Paige Cognetti, the Democratic mayor of Scranton, 46 percent to 51 percent. Ms. Cognetti and her supporters have run numerous ads accusing Mr. Bresnahan of profiting from insider stock trading, and voters in Pennsylvania gave her an 11-point edge when asked which candidate they would trust to handle corruption.

In Pennsylvania’s Seventh District, Representative Ryan Mackenzie, a Republican, is behind his Democratic rival, Bob Brooks, the head of a local firefighters union, by five points. In 2024, Mr. Trump won the swing district by three points, and Mr. Mackenzie prevailed by one point.

The survey in the diverse district also found that Mr. Brooks had a wide lead among nonwhite voters, as both candidates court the Hispanic vote in cities such as Allentown.

The other two races are closer.

In Pennsylvania’s 10th District, Representative Scott Perry, a Republican, is tied at 48 percent with Janelle Stelson, a Democrat and former news broadcaster, in a rematch of their 2024 race. Ms. Stelson is favored on the issue that voters said they cared most about — the cost of living — but it has not so far been enough to pull away from Mr. Perry in a district where he is still favored on immigration.

In Pennsylvania’s First District, Representative Brian Fitzpatrick, the Republican, trails his Democratic challenger, Bob Harvie, a local county commissioner in Bucks County, 46 percent to 48 percent. This seat is the mostDemocratic of the four, and Mr. Fitzpatrick is one of only three current House Republicans to represent a district that Mr. Trump lost in 2024.

Money has poured into the race in recent weeks, as Democrats believe this is the year they will finally be able to defeat Mr. Fitzpatrick, who has defied his district’s Democratic lean in presidential elections for a decade.

On the issues, voters repeatedly say they trust Mr. Harvie more. Even on immigration, traditionally an area where Republicans excel, the Democrat has a two-point advantage.

The New York TimesPhiladelphia InquirerSiena University poll

Oct. 16-22

Based on a New York Times/Philadelphia Inquirer/Siena poll of 1,607 likely voters across four Pennsylvania congressional districts conducted Oct. 16 to 22. Question wording has been condensed.

Jillian Vordick/The New York Times

And voters worry that the Republican Mr. Fitzpatrick, whose district has voted against Mr. Trump for president each time Mr. Fitzpatrick has appeared on the ballot, is too cozy with the president. Nearly half of voters said they were worried that Mr. Fitzpatrick was too supportive of Mr. Trump.

Still, Mr. Fitzpatrick is holding his own in the fight for his political life, boosted by the support of 20 percent of voters who say they plan to support Josh Shapiro, the popular Democratic governor who is running for re-election.

All told, across these four congressional races, roughly $100 million in advertising is set to have aired since the start of September, according to the ad-tracking service AdImpact.

Overall, Mr. Trump is unpopular in the districts represented by the four seats, with a 39 percent overall approval rating. Though low, it is higher than his approval rating nationally or statewide in Pennsylvania. Democrats are hoping to take advantage of a favorable political environment.

Mr. Shapiro, who has run well ahead of his Republican challenger, Stacy Garrity, this year, is leading her by 18 points across the four districts, similar to his 19-point margin statewide in a September Times/Inquirer/Siena poll.

But even as Mr. Shapiro is peeling off the support of about 15 percent of Republicans in these districts, those voters appear poised to split their tickets and back G.O.P. candidates in their home communities.

Mr. Perry, who is the former chairman of the hard-right House Freedom Caucus, has aggressively defended the war in Iran and backed many of Mr. Trump’s signature policies.

Of the four districts polled, Mr. Trump appears to be the most popular in Mr. Perry’s district. Half of voters there said they approved of the president’s approach on immigration, including 44 percent of political independents.

Voters also seemed to back the Republican Mr. Perry’s support for the president. More said they trusted Mr. Perry to handle immigration and foreign wars, even as Ms. Stelson enjoyed a substantial advantage on cost of living, with more voters saying they would trust her to “do what’s best for ordinary Pennsylvanians.”

Across the four key battlegrounds, economic issues ranked as the most important: 25 percent of voters rated the economy as their top issue, and another 13 percent said that the cost of living or inflation was the most important. No other issue cracked double digits.

Mr. Trump had a 32 percent approval rating when it came to how he was handling the cost of living. Yet the Democratic congressional candidates had only a six-point edge over the Republican incumbents on the issue.

Voter dissatisfaction with Mr. Trump, though, is broadly apparent in the polls.

In the four districts, half of white voters without a college degree — a contingent that is the backbone of Mr. Trump’s base and a decisive voting bloc in Pennsylvania — disapproved of Mr. Trump’s job performance. Sixty percent disapproved of his handling of cost of living.

That dissatisfaction with Mr. Trump’s approach to economic issues among white working-class voters is playing out across the country.

The Democratic candidates in Pennsylvania are not winning among white voters without a college degree. But the 40 percent support they are garnering is a noteworthy incursion into what has typically been the base of the Republican Party during the Trump era.

Overall, Ms. Cognetti had the most favorable image of the eight candidates for the four seats. By a margin of 10 points, more viewed her favorably than unfavorably. That was far better than her opponent, Mr. Bresnahan, who had a net favorability rating of just one point. Particularly concerning for Republicans is his favorability among political independents — a crucial group — with whom he is underwater by 13 points.

Voters also have concerns about Mr. Bresnahan’s character. He is tied for the lowest rating among the eight candidates — 39 percent — when it comes to who voters think has strong character. Ms. Cognetti, on the other hand, tops the list. Half of voters in the Eighth District, including 11 percent of Republicans, said the Democratic Ms. Cognetti had better character than Mr. Bresnahan.

Across all the issues included in the poll, Democrats held one of their widest leads when it came to who voters trusted to address the growing concern about data centers used to power artificial intelligence. In the Seventh District, where data centers have become a central issue, Mr. Brooks had a 10-point advtange over Mr. Mackenzie.

The polls, though, suggest that the issue — despite its prominence in recent television ads — may not be decisive. Just 2 percent of voters listed A.I. or data centers as their top issue.

Here are the key things to know about these New York Times/Philadelphia Inquirer/Siena polls:

The Times/Siena polls of Pennsylvania in 2026 were conducted in partnership with The Philadelphia Inquirer and were funded in part by a grant from the Lenfest Institute for Journalism. The polls were designed and conducted independently from the institute.

You can see full results and a detailed methodology here. If you want to read more about how and why we conduct our polls, you can see answers to frequently asked questions and submit your own questions here.

item.title: In Texas, Talarico Leans Into Growing Rivalry With Elon Musk
item.description:
A rivalry between the world’s richest person and one of the most prominent Democratic candidates is intensifying during the final stage of this year’s midterm elections.

On the campaign trail in Texas, James Talarico, the Democratic nominee for Senate, is increasingly criticizing Elon Musk over his role in the race. Mr. Musk made a huge contribution this fall to a group aligned with Ken Paxton, Mr. Talarico’s Republican opponent, recent campaign finance disclosures showed.

The race in Texas, a pivotal contest that could determine control of the Senate, is now in part a test of whether Democrats can turn Mr. Musk into a political boogeyman and whether his infusion of cash can lift a Republican candidate who has lagged behind his opponent in fund-raising.

“Elon Musk wants our land. He wants our water. He wants our tax dollars,” Mr. Talarico said at a rally in San Antonio on Saturday, as the crowd booed in disapproval of Mr. Musk. “He wants his very own personal United States senator.”

Representatives for Mr. Musk and Mr. Paxton did not respond to requests for comment.

Mr. Talarico has stepped up his attacks on Mr. Musk after campaign finance filings revealed earlier this month that Mr. Musk, a Texas resident who has major business interests in the state, donated $158 million to a Republican super PAC that then flipped the same amount to a group allied with Mr. Paxton.

At the University of Texas on Friday, Mr. Talarico said Mr. Musk was trying to “stop the movement that we are building in our state.” The day before that, Mr. Talarico’s campaign released a digital advertisement accusing Mr. Paxton of being beholden to Mr. Musk. “Let’s remind Elon: Texas is not for sale,” says the narrator of the ad.

Mr. Talarico is betting that Mr. Musk’s connection to the contest will hurt Mr. Paxton. It’s not the first time Democrats have made such a wager.

Last year, Mr. Musk and allied groups spent more than $20 million boosting a conservative Wisconsin Supreme Court candidate, who ended up losing to a liberal opponent. Mr. Musk’s efforts, which included campaigning in the state, may have backfired, inflaming Democratic anger as the race increasingly became a referendum on his influence in U.S. government and the slashing of the federal work force that he oversaw.

Other candidates have also tried to channel anger against an onslaught of outside spending to their advantage.

During Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary, Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, who ultimately won the party’s nomination, repeatedly attacked his rival, Representative Haley Stevens, over the more than $30 million that groups linked to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee poured into ads boosting her run.

In polls and focus groups in Texas, voters have voiced concerns about corruption and the influence of the wealthy and powerful in politics, said Matt Angle, a Democratic strategist in the state. He argued that Mr. Musk “has made himself the face of” what some voters perceive as the Republican Party’s fealty to megadonors.

At Mr. Talarico’s rally on Saturday, the crowd roared when he brought up Mr. Musk and cheered loudly when he said his own campaign is “funded by 1.3 million individuals who have donated their hard-earned money.”

Mr. Musk has not campaigned with Mr. Paxton. But he has publicly endorsed him and has used his platform on X, the social media company he owns, to attack Mr. Talarico with growing frequency. Mr. Musk posted on X about Mr. Talarico 18 times last week, claiming Mr. Talarico “hates Texas” and disparaging him in other ways.

JT Ennis, a spokesman for Mr. Talarico, said Mr. Musk’s immense spending in the race “isn’t working, so he’s throwing a tantrum.”

For his part, Mr. Paxton speaks about Mr. Musk rarely, if ever, on the trail. But in a recent fund-raising email to supporters, Mr. Paxton praised him.

“Democrats are trying to buy President Trump’s Senate Majority,” Paxton says in the Thursday email, adding, “But Elon Musk REFUSES to let them get away with it.” Mr. Paxton wrote that he was “proud to have Elon’s support at this do-or-die moment in the election.”

Mr. Talarico’s campaign has vastly out-raised Mr. Paxton’s. And for months, Mr. Paxton and his allies had relatively little money to spend on advertisements. But in September, Mr. Trump’s super PAC and a series of groups linked to Mr. Musk and Senate Republicans dumped tens of millions of dollars into outside advertising for Mr. Paxton, hoping to rescue the Republican’s bid to hold the seat for his party.

Mr. Talarico has eschewed corporate PAC money, largely raising small-dollar donations. When criticized for billionaires’ donations to super PACs backing his run, he has responded that outside groups cannot coordinate with campaigns.

At a Paxton rally in Georgetown on Saturday, Republicans had mixed feelings about Mr. Musk’s support. George Gutierrez, 72, who is semiretired and lives in Round Rock, said he was comfortable with the alliance between Mr. Musk and Mr. Paxton.

Bobby Bagwell, 54, expressed discomfort with the idea of the ultrawealthy playing a major role in financing campaigns. But he said it was disingenuous of Mr. Talarico to criticize wealthy donors getting involved in politics when they have given to groups supporting his candidacy.

“I don’t like the idea of a bunch of superrich billionaires throwing their money around,” said Mr. Bagwell, a home-builder who lives in Leander.

Lauren McGaughy contributed reporting from Austin and Georgetown, Texas, and Marisela Cruz contributed reporting from San Antonio.

item.title: Alaska Democrat Postpones Events After ‘Minor Injuries’ in Automobile Collision, Campaign Says
item.description:
Former Representative Mary Peltola, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Alaska, a pivotal race, is postponing planned campaign events for Sunday and Monday after sustaining “minor injuries that required medical attention” following an automobile collision on Saturday night, according to her campaign.

The vehicle that Ms. Peltola and her family were in was struck by another driver, Ms. Peltola’s campaign said in a news release. They were en route to the Alaska Federation of Natives annual banquet in Anchorage, a gathering of the state’s largest organization of Native American tribes.

“Mary and her family sustained minor injuries but are in good spirits,” Cheryl Bruce, Ms. Peltola’s campaign manager, said in a statement.

Ms. Peltola announced a seven-day campaign blitz on Saturday, calling it the “Alaska Always Tour.” On the advice of medical professionals, she is rescheduling events in Fairbanks and Bethel for later in the week, Ms. Bruce said in her statement. The events were previously scheduled to take place on Sunday and Monday. Other events will continue on schedule, the campaign said.

When asked for additional information about the incident, Ms. Peltola’s campaign pointed to the statement from Ms. Bruce and declined to comment further. The authorities did not immediately provide more details about the incident.

Ms. Peltola is challenging Senator Dan S. Sullivan, a Republican seeking a third term, in a race seen as a key battleground in the fight for control of the Senate.

The Alaska race has come under a national spotlight in recent days. The Department of Justice on Thursday asked a federal court to block the certification of the results if Mr. Sullivan loses narrowly, an extraordinary step that President Trump said he ordered.

The Justice Department argued that voters’ confusion over another Republican candidate with the same name as the incumbent — except for a middle initial — could unfairly sway the election. The lawsuit is viewed as highly unlikely to succeed, in part because Alaska’s Supreme Court already ruled that both Mr. Sullivans may remain on the ballot.

Kellen Browning and Evan Gorelick contributed reporting.

item.title: Trump’s Election Attacks Enter New Pre-emptive Phase
item.description:
For months, President Trump has mounted a sustained effort to attack the integrity of U.S. elections while using the federal government to try to assert more control over the voting process overseen by states.

Last week, Mr. Trump opened a new front.

Rather than simply push false claims at his rallies or target voters his administration claims should not be on the rolls, Mr. Trump moved to pre-emptively challenge the certification of Alaska’s Senate election if the Republican candidate narrowly loses.

In doing so, Mr. Trump harnessed the power of the federal government to try to interfere in the voting process before Election Day — essentially trying to nullify an opponent’s potential win before the game has been called.

Even for a president who worked to undermine and overturn the 2020 presidential election, the anticipatory strike reflects a new intensification of Mr. Trump’s attempts to use his official powers to achieve the election results he wants — one that undermines the democratic process, according to election and legal experts. While they say the administration’s lawsuit is unlikely to be successful, the tactic could still further Mr. Trump’s goals by shaking the confidence of voters in the outcome of the race.

“This is part of the election takeover playbook that I’ve seen around the world and unfortunately in some other autocratic environments,” said Michael McNulty, a former senior elections adviser for the U.S. Agency for International Development who has studied election issues around the world, including in El Salvador, Hungary and Venezuela. “Trump has essentially undermined the independence of the D.O.J. and it’s been weaponized.”

The latest phase of Mr. Trump’s strategy centers on the Justice Department, which asked a federal court to block the certification of the election if the Republican incumbent, Senator Dan S. Sullivan, were to lose by a slim margin. The administration argued the presence of another candidate with a nearly identical name on the ballot has skewed the election toward Democrats.

The issue has already been litigated in the state: In June, the Alaska Supreme Court ruled that Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., a retired elementary schoolteacher, could appear on the ballot.

But Attorney General Todd Blanche maintained on Sunday that the federal government had a role in inserting itself into the process.

“We’re not saying that the federal government is going to decide who the next senator from Alaska is,” Mr. Blanche said on CNN’s “State of the Union.” He added: “But if it’s clear that there was confusion and that confusion led to an unjust, improper result that is not the will of the Alaskan voters, we want to make sure that the Alaskan system and the Alaskan state courts and the Alaskan electoral process can understand that in a way that lets them do the right thing.”

When asked for comment, the White House referred to an exchange Mr. Trump had with reporters on Saturday about his administration’s efforts to intervene in Alaska, a lawsuit he said was made at his direction. Republicans have asserted that the candidacy of the second Mr. Sullivan is a Democratic scheme to confuse voters. Democrats have said they have no connection to that candidate, who will appear on the ballot without any party affiliation and has said he is running genuine campaign.

“It is a totally corrupt weaponization situation, and they shouldn’t be allowed to do it,” Mr. Trump said of the Democrats in Alaska. “So I recommended it to the D.O.J. They looked at it, they agreed with me, and they’ve gone to court. Let’s see what happens. But that’s pure corruption.”

Election law specialists say Mr. Trump’s lawsuit in Alaska lacks legal basis and will likely fail. But that might not be the point.

The lawsuit is just one piece of a blitz of federal actions by the Trump administration to assert more control over the electoral process that have run into court challenges. Mr. Trump introduced a plan to have the U.S. Postal Service screen mail ballots, only to have it be blocked by the Supreme Court.

The administration has sued 30 states and the District of Columbia for refusing to cede to the federal government’s demands to turn over voter rolls. The administration has lost 27 of those cases. The other cases are pending.

Mr. Trump has deployed homeland security investigators to find evidence of illegal voting in states where it has claimed without evidence there is widespread noncitizen voting. A federal judge restricted much of that effort this week.

But with each claim of election fraud, Mr. Trump is creating another platform to sow doubt about the elections and, some state officials and election experts worry, lay the groundwork to challenge the results of the specific contests.

“The goal is obviously not to win the legal case because if so, that would be a complete failure because it’s going to fail,” said Mr. McNulty, senior policy director for Issue One, a nonpartisan group that tracks election issues. “The goal is to create doubt about the process and then use that doubt to justify later intervention or interference.”

Mr. Trump’s frequent attacks on the security of voting machines have raised fears among congressional Democrats and some election officials that he could be setting the stage to contest the results of the November elections.

The lawsuit in Alaska has added a new layer to those worries. The federal challenge could give cover to officials in the state to question the results of the election, experts warned.

The state’s Division of Elections is overseen by Alaska’s lieutenant governor, a Republican, who initially gave the green light to remove the second Mr. Sullivan from the ballot before he was reinstated by the courts. The lieutenant governor, Nancy Dahlstrom, previously challenged Representative Mary S. Peltola, Mr. Sullivan’s primary Democratic opponent in the senate race, for her House seat.

Mr. Trump has installed allies throughout the federal government who have echoed his false claims about voting. And across the country, a number of local election officials who have expressed sympathy with the election-denier movement now occupy key posts.

Benjamin Hovland, who was ousted by Mr. Trump from the independent, bipartisan federal Election Assistance Commission earlier this year, said he worried the various actions by the administration were serving a pretext for lawsuits after Election Day, based on dubious claims of noncitizen voting and fraud in the electoral process.

“What the D.O.J. is tipping its hand to is stepping in as essentially the president’s personal law firm to try to undercut the credibility of election results they don’t like,” Mr. Hovland said. “And that is a pretty horrible prospect.”

Alan Feuer contributed reporting.

]]>

item.title: Catholic Leaders Say Meeting With Trump Wasn’t Intended to Be Political
item.description:
The video, not even 30 seconds long, showed several Roman Catholic bishops praying with President Trump last week in the Oval Office.

That footage, shared on social media by a White House official during the thick of election season, blazed across the internet and became entangled in the fractured politics of the country and the church.

Archbishop James R. Golka of Denver, who led the prayer, told a local Catholic publication that it “was never my intention” for the meeting to be seen as an endorsement.

One attendee, Bishop William Joensen of Des Moines, wrote afterward that “I wish I had been more shrewd and less simple, like those who exploited our meeting for partisan political purposes.”

Another, Archbishop Jeffrey S. Grob of Milwaukee, publicly apologized on Sunday and claimed that the video had been shared by the White House without the bishops’ permission.

“I feel a heavy sadness, not only over the pain I caused, but also for the fact that something so sacred to a group of religious leaders, prayer to our Heavenly Father, would be manipulated in that way,” Archbishop Grob wrote in an open letter. He added: “We should never have been put in that position by the White House.”

White House officials did not directly comment on Archbishop Grob’s claim that the video was shared without permission.

“There has never been a greater president for Catholic Americans than President Trump, and his strong record proves it,” Taylor Rogers, a White House spokeswoman, said in a statement when asked about the meeting. She said that the president had pardoned anti-abortion activists, “proudly defended and expanded our religious rights” and “stopped the weaponization of the federal government against Christians.”

The prayer itself — at least the snippet of it shared by the White House — was not explicitly political.

Archbishop Golka, with his hand on Mr. Trump’s shoulder, said, “Thank you for the gift of our great beautiful nation; thank you for the gift of our government; thank you for the gift of this office of presidency. We lift up our president and ask your blessing upon him.”

The video, posted on X by the White House official Margo Martin, appeared to start mid-prayer and seemed to end before the archbishop had finished. Footage of the meeting was also posted on a Facebook page for Mr. Trump’s political operation with the caption, “FAITH FRIDAYS: This White House prays together.”

American Catholics are politically mixed.

Pew Research Center data from 2023 found that about 52 percent of Catholics were Republicans or leaned Republican, and 44 percent were Democrats or leaned toward Democrats. Former President Joseph R. Biden Jr., a Democrat, and Vice President JD Vance, a Republican, are both Catholic.

Catholic leaders have historically called out presidential administrations of both parties for actions seen as contrary to the church’s teachings. Mr. Biden was often criticized for his support for abortion rights. And Pope Leo XIV, the first American pontiff, has often been publicly at odds with Mr. Trump.

Last year, Archbishop Grob and other Wisconsin bishops signed a letter voicing “strong concern regarding the indiscriminate nature of the current federal immigration enforcement.”

In his apology on Sunday, Archbishop Grob said he had been joined by 11 other bishops at the White House in a meeting organized by the Heritage Foundation, a conservative group.

Archbishop Grob said he had been “told the meeting was to be a private discussion, that several Catholic members of the cabinet might make an appearance, and that there could be an opportunity to pray privately with the president.” He said he had not intended to endorse “the president, his policies or his party.”

“We came in good faith to try to work for the betterment of our fellow human beings, to ease their suffering, to build up the common good and to pray with a president, not to pose for a political photo opportunity to benefit the few,” Archbishop Grob wrote.

Bishop Joensen of Des Moines wrote that “there are many things tied to this present administration that are blatantly at odds with our Catholic faith,” but that he often engages with officials who hold differing views.

“None of us bishops were unaware that our meeting was on the cusp of a national election,” Bishop Joensen wrote. “Yet in no way did any of us intend by our involvement to endorse any political party or any individual candidate. That said, in retrospect, I would have done well to be more mindful of Jesus’ admonition: ‘Behold, I am sending you like sheep in the midst of wolves; so be shrewd as serpents and simple as doves.’”

In an interview with Denver Catholic, an archdiocese publication, Archbishop Golka described praying about the invitation.

“Though I originally thought it would be a private meeting, I knew that it could be shared and that some might use it for political purposes,” the archbishop said. “But as I prayed about it, I thought that this is what Catholics do. We pray for people. No matter whether we agree or disagree on anything, we always pray for our country and leaders.”
